strengths: Clear problem formulation identifying the gap between didactic expert solutions and model-generated reasoning, with insightful distinction between didactic and rationalization shortcuts
Thoughtful technical design combining mixed policy rollouts with contrastive learning in a practical offline framework; LoRA-based memory efficiency is well-engineered

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (AIME 2024/25, BeyondAIME, IMO-AnswerBench, GPQA-Diamond) with extensive baselines (GRPO, NuRL, STaR, temperature variations) and thorough ablations (Figures 5-7)

Strong and consistent empirical results: 10-25% pass@k improvements on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, 2-4× token efficiency gains, with <1000 expert examples demonstrating practical sample efficiency
Honest acknowledgment of limitations: Figure 16 and Section B.6 candidly show method fails on weaker models (Qwen3-4B, Deepseek-R1), defining clear applicability boundaries
Good reproducibility foundation: extensive appendices with hyperparameters, prompts, generation procedures, training curves; commitment to release datasets and code
Analysis of train-test generalization gap (Figure 6) effectively demonstrates that contrastive loss prevents shortcut memorization while NLL and RLVR baselines overfit
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core components (mixed policy decoding from speculative decoding, contrastive learning from Kumar et al. 2022, interactive imitation from DAgger) are well-established; contribution is primarily in combination rather than innovation

Contrastive loss lacks theoretical justification: negative divergence term is unbounded (acknowledged by authors); stability justified only empirically through initialization. No principled analysis of why this loss specifically targets rationalization shortcuts

Negative reference construction is overly domain-specific: regex-based waypoint extraction (numbers, exponentials, symbolic coefficients) only works for mathematics; no sensitivity analysis or generalization to other domains demonstrated despite claims of broad applicability

Dataset curation introduces potential biases: e1-verifiable selected based on model failures (32 attempts) rather than difficulty, potentially selecting edge cases; only 417/669 problems from single sources with limited diversity; 15 overlapping problems with evaluation set (IMO-AnswerBench) raise leakage concerns

Insufficient analysis of generated traces: no qualitative evaluation of expansion validity; Figure 12 shows 4× length increase but no investigation of whether expansion is necessary or contains spurious details; missing error analysis of what shortcuts contrastive loss actually prevents

Hyperparameter tuning concerns: τ calibrated on training set performance (Figure 11) invites overfitting; γ tuned on small 100-sample validation set; Figure 16 suggests γ=0.1 may be suboptimal for smaller models but retuning not attempted; raises generalization questions

Weak out-of-domain generalization evidence: Table 1 (GPQA-Diamond) shows DAIL only marginally outperforms or underperforms baseline; claims about preserving 'fundamental reasoning capabilities' unsupported; only one OOD domain tested against mathematics-focused training

Model competence requirement severely limits applicability: Figure 16 shows complete failure on weaker models (Qwen3-4B, Deepseek-R1); explanation (weak instruction-following, dense shortcuts) is hand-wavy; method requires already-capable frontier models

Baseline implementation concerns: GRPO/NuRL appear to be authors' implementations with unclear tuning effort; NuRL 'ineffective' despite convergence—unclear if fair comparison or implementation issue; RLVR degradation on hard problems may reflect algorithm limitations rather than DAIL superiority

Missing efficiency details: data generation computational cost not quantified; dual-model inference in mixed policy rollouts adds overhead not discussed; '2-4× fewer tokens' claim lacks detail on output quality equivalence across different models

Incomplete reproducibility documentation: code/dataset links in footnotes are absent or incomplete and not verifiable; mixed policy verification condition (τ application to log vs. raw probability) not specified; 256-token truncation bias for reasoning models not analyzed
Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; some reported differences are small; single runs reported; variance not quantified across multiple seeds

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies and articulates the distribution mismatch between expert solutions and model reasoning, with compelling intuition for why behavioral cloning fails
Novel technical approach: The privileged student + contrastive learning combination is creative; mixed policy rollouts cleverly preserve authentic reasoning while grounding in expert solutions
Strong empirical results: Consistent 10-25% pass@k improvements across AIME, BeyondAIME, and IMO-AnswerBench; first demonstration of improving long-CoT reasoning from expert solutions

Rigorous experimental methodology: Comprehensive baselines, thoughtful ablations (Figures 5-7), and compelling analysis showing DAIL learns generalizable patterns versus baselines that overfit to training data (Figure 6)
Practical value and sample efficiency: Works with <1000 expensive expert solutions; offline formulation enables parallelization; 2-4× efficiency gains and 0.1 H100-hours/epoch vs 277.6 for GRPO
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-written with effective visualizations; comprehensive appendices; novel dataset (e1-proof) to be released; good implementation details
Out-of-domain generalization: Maintains or improves performance on GPQA-Diamond; results suggest no catastrophic forgetting
weaknesses: Limited generalization beyond mathematics: Method is developed/evaluated primarily on math; negative reference uses hand-crafted regex patterns (numbers, exponentials, coefficients); unclear how to apply to other domains (code, science, etc.); only brief out-of-domain evaluation

Requires competent base models: Figure 16 shows DAIL fails or provides minimal benefit on weaker models (Qwen3-4B, Deepseek-R1); no clear guidance on minimum capability thresholds; significantly constrains applicability

Weak theoretical justification: Contrastive loss stability justified empirically ('we find training remains stable') not theoretically; choice of KL divergence not well motivated; design appears somewhat ad-hoc despite good motivation
Hyperparameter tuning on small validation sets: γ tuned on 100-sample validation set; τ on training set only; high risk of overfitting and poor generalization across models/domains

Data leakage and deduplication concerns: 15 problems (3.75%) in IMO-AnswerBench overlap with training data; SentenceBERT deduplication threshold (0.7) is arbitrary; while addressed, raises experimental rigor questions

Limited mechanical analysis of learned representations: No qualitative examples of improved reasoning; missing analysis of how expert methodology transfers to student; essentially 'black box' evaluation
Domain-specific design limits applicability: Prompts are math-specific (Figures 8-10); negative reference regex patterns don't generalize; method appears tightly coupled to mathematical reasoning

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the practical challenge of learning from expensive, didactic expert solutions through a clear two-stage approach with comprehensive experimental validation
Efficient offline training enabling parallelization (0.1 vs. 277.6 H100 hours per epoch vs. GRPO) and strong empirical results showing up to 31% pass@128 gains and 2× reasoning efficiency

Thorough experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (AIME 2024/2025, BeyondAIME, IMO-AnswerBench, GPQA-Diamond) with rigorous ablations (Figures 5-7) demonstrating necessity of each component and out-of-domain generalization
Enables learning on non-verifiable problems where RLVR cannot apply, demonstrated by consistent improvements on long-CoT Olympiad proofs across varying token budgets

Clear presentation with excellent visualization (Figure 1), detailed appendices with reproducibility information (hyperparameters, prompts, generation details), and public dataset contribution (e1-proof)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (self-distillation from Yang et al. 2024, speculative decoding, interactive imitation, contrastive learning) in relatively straightforward manner; concurrent work (Zhao et al. 2026, Hubotter et al. 2026, Shenfeld et al. 2026) doing similar things substantially weakens originality claim

Weak theoretical justification: contrastive loss intuition is provided but not rigorously justified; claim about training stability despite unbounded divergence term is hand-wavy (§2.2); no formal analysis of optimal negative reference construction via partial solutions

Significant generalization limitations: method requires competent models (Table 11 shows degradation on Llama-3.1-8B), negative reference construction is domain-specific (math-specific regex patterns; minimal improvements on HealthBench per Appendix B), and heavy reliance on prompt engineering reduces transferability

Dataset leakage issue: 15 problems from test set IMO-AnswerBench overlap with training set e1-verifiable, discovered post-hoc and addressed only by showing results are 'robust' (Figure 14) rather than preventing leakage a priori; deduplication only initially done for e1-proof

Incomplete performance analysis: contrastive loss provides only ~5-15% pass@1 gain over NLL (Figure 5), underperforming distillation from larger models at high token budgets (Table 10: 49 vs. 55 at 4096 tokens), and missing ablation disentangling contribution of expanded traces vs. contrastive loss

Evaluation methodology concerns: post-hoc evaluation configuration changes (C.1) to handle >10% non-response rates suggest mid-review methodological modifications; τ hyperparameter chosen on training set rather than held-out validation; γ tuned on only 100-sample validation set; different epoch counts (5 vs. 3) across models appear ad-hoc

Limited theoretical understanding and exploration: on-policy variants dismissed due to slow convergence (C.7) without thorough investigation despite concurrent work showing promise; no qualitative analysis of what reasoning patterns are learned; no failure case analysis or sample efficiency curves

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real challenge where RLVR fails on hard problems and direct fine-tuning on expert solutions causes performance degradation
Coherent technical approach combining mixed policy rollouts with contrastive learning, where each component addresses a specific issue (didactic vs. rationalization shortcuts)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (e1-verifiable: 417 problems, e1-proof: 669), benchmarks (AIME, BeyondAIME, IMO-AnswerBench, GPQA), and models (Qwen2.5, Qwen3-8B/14B, DeepSeek-R1)
Strong empirical results: up to 31% pass@128 gains, 2× reasoning efficiency (achieves same performance with half tokens), enables learning on non-verifiable problems for LRMs
Excellent reproducibility with code/datasets released, comprehensive implementation details in appendix, documented hyperparameters, and training curves
Novel contribution of enabling long-CoT reasoning improvement from expert solutions without reward models
Practical efficiency gains: 0.1 H100 hours per epoch vs. 277.6 for GRPO, with LoRA reducing memory requirements
Meaningful ablations (Figures 5-7, Tables 9) support design choices and show contrastive loss outperforms NLL baseline
weaknesses: Limited novelty of individual components: mixed policy rollouts adapt speculative decoding, self-distillation for distribution alignment explored in Yang et al. (2024), contrastive learning for shortcuts is straightforward; contribution is primarily in combination

Significant data quality concerns: IMO-AnswerBench contains 15 problems 'sharing underlying sources' with e1-verifiable, discovered post-hoc rather than pre-experimentally; while Figure 14 shows minimal impact, this undermines reproducibility claims
Hyperparameter tuning on insufficiently small validation sets: γ tuned on 100-sample set, τ calibrated on training set only, raising overfitting concerns and limiting reproducibility

Strong model and domain dependencies: method fails on weaker models (Llama-3.1-8B degrades in Table 11), non-math domains show only marginal improvements (Tables 2-5), negative reference construction is regex-based and math-specific

Lacks theoretical grounding: contrastive loss has no convergence analysis, unbounded negative divergence term justified only empirically (Figure 13), no formal analysis of why this objective prevents shortcuts
Insufficient analysis of learned behaviors: no qualitative examples of prevented shortcuts, no error analysis or failure modes, no comparison of generation strategies between DAIL and baselines
Mixed out-of-domain generalization: GPQA-Diamond Table 1 shows pass@1 degradation for Qwen2.5 (34.1→35.1), contradicting 'maintains or improves' claim

Unclear positioning relative to concurrent work: multiple concurrent self-distillation papers (Zhao et al., Hubotter et al., Shenfeld et al., 2026) address similar problems; differences and advantages over concurrent approaches are vague
Limited dataset scale and scope: e1-verifiable contains only 417 problems, both datasets are specialized (math/Olympiad), limiting generalizability beyond reasoning domains

Arbitrary design choices: 256-token truncation for reasoning model rollouts is unexplained; sensitivity to τ hyperparameter (Figure 11) suggests method requires careful tuning; different optimal epochs for different models (5 vs 3) suggests fragility
